haiku-low.q1: They do not differ. Both return the same status, page, headers and no Set-Cookie, with the message Invalid email or password. The app also runs bcrypt either way, using a dummy hash when no row exists.
haiku-low.q2: The server returns 429 with Retry-After and does not check the password. The attempt is not recorded and the lock does not extend.
haiku-low.q3: The session named by the incoming cookie is deleted first. A new session with a new sid is created and set in a new cookie.
haiku-low.q4: Only the random session ID (sid), 43 base64url characters. The cookie is HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it.
haiku-low.q5: The 12-hour absolute cap still applies: it stops at login time plus 12 hours, even with constant use. Idle expiry (30 minutes) is refreshed on each request, so it does not end an active session.
haiku-low.q6: It redirects to /login and clears the cookie. Expired and unknown session IDs both count as signed out.
haiku-low.q7: The server deletes the session key before replying, and only if a cookie is present. If it is already gone, the response is the same, and the cookie is cleared and the user redirected to /login.
haiku-low.q8: Sessions are kept in one new Redis instance on the private network. Any app instance finds one by looking up the hash of the sid in Redis, with no sticky sessions needed.
haiku-low.q9: In a Redis sorted set named fail: plus the email's SHA-256 hash, with failure timestamps as members. Each write trims entries older than 10 minutes, so only the remaining entries are counted.
haiku-low.q10: It compares the current time with abs_exp. If the session is valid, it resets the Redis key TTL to the smaller of 30 minutes and the time left until abs_exp.
haiku-low.q11: The browser gets 503 and no session is created. The failed attempt is also not recorded.
haiku-low.q12: No sweeper job exists. Redis TTLs delete the keys: sessions within 30 minutes, failure sets 10 minutes after their last entry, and locks after 15 minutes.

sonnet.q1: It doesn't differ. Status, page, headers and body must match exactly (401 login page, 'Invalid email or password', no Set-Cookie). bcrypt runs against a dummy hash so timing is similar too.
sonnet.q2: The email is locked (15-minute lock set by the 5th failure). The attempt gets 429 with Retry-After, the password is not checked, the attempt is not recorded and the lock does not extend.
sonnet.q3: On a successful login the old session (named by the cookie) is deleted from Redis, and a new session with a new sid is created and set in the cookie.
sonnet.q4: Only the random session ID (sid, 256 random bits, 43 base64url chars). No user data. Scripts cannot read it because the cookie is HttpOnly.
sonnet.q5: After 12 hours from login (abs_exp, the absolute cap). Idle expiry (30 min) keeps being refreshed by activity, but the absolute expiry is checked on every request.
sonnet.q6: It redirects (302) to /login and clears the cookie. If abs_exp has passed, it also deletes the session key. (If Redis errors instead, it returns 503 and keeps the cookie.)
sonnet.q7: If a cookie is present, the server deletes the session key in Redis and only then replies with 302 to /login and clears the cookie. If the session is already gone, the delete does nothing and the response is the same. If Redis fails, it returns 503 and keeps the cookie.
sonnet.q8: In Redis, shared by both instances, under key sess: plus SHA-256 of the sid. Any instance takes the sid from the cookie, hashes it, and looks up that key in Redis.
sonnet.q9: In a Redis sorted set fail: plus SHA-256 of the lowercased email, whose members are timestamps of failures. On each write a Lua script trims entries older than 10 minutes, adds the new timestamp and counts the remaining entries.
sonnet.q10: It checks that the session key exists in Redis and that the current time is before abs_exp. When valid, it runs EXPIRE on the session key, resetting the TTL to min(30 min, abs_exp minus now).
sonnet.q11: A 503 (sign-in temporarily unavailable). No session is created and the failure is not recorded.
sonnet.q12: Redis TTL expiry. Each session key has an idle TTL of at most 30 minutes, and Redis deletes it on its own. There is no sweeper job.
